extracted.intended_audience: editors, copyeditors, authors, and publishers (University of Chicago Press style users)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for capitalization, italics, quotations, spelling, abbreviations, and conventions used in preparing scholarly and general prose for publication according to the University of Chicago Press Manual of Style.

rubrics_metrics.name: 44. Titles of ancient manuscripts (MS; MSS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the definite article as part of the title; singular MS, plural MSS for ancient manuscripts (see 60).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Chicago Tribune, the School Review; Codex Bernensis, Cod. Canonicianus.

rubrics_metrics.name: 45. Capitalization in hyphenated titles' nouns
rubrics_metrics.description: In titles with main words capitalized, capitalize all nouns forming parts of hyphenated compounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "Twentieth-Century Progress," "The Economy of High-Speed Trains." Do not capitalize non-noun components: "Fifty-first Street," "Lives of Well-known Authors," "World-Dominion of English-speaking Peoples."

rubrics_metrics.name: 46. Scientific (Latin) names capitalization in botanical/geological/zoological/paleontological matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Use capitals for scientific (Latin) names of divisions, orders, families, genera; do not capitalize their English derivatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cotylosauria (but cotylosaurs); Felidae (but felids); Carnivora (but carnivores). Species names derived from persons or from generic names may be capitalized in botanical/zoological contexts but not usually in geological/medical contexts. Examples: Felis leo, Cocos nudifera, Rosa Carolina; geological examples: Pterygomatopus schmidti, Conodectus favosus. See also rule 71.

rubrics_metrics.name: 47. Capitalize names and epithets of peoples, races, tribes
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names and epithets of peoples, races, and tribes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Kafir, Negro (in its ethnical sense), Hottentot, Makassar, Buginese, Celestials.

rubrics_metrics.name: 48. Capitalization in astronomical work
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of bodies of our solar system except 'sun,' 'earth,' 'moon,' and 'stars'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Milky Way, the Great Bear, Saturn.

rubrics_metrics.name: 49. Capitalization of University divisions, departments, officers, courses (official work)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize divisions, departments, officers, and courses of study of the University of Chicago in official administrative or curricular contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the School of Education (the School), the University Extension Division (but: the division), Department of Anthropology (but: the department), Board of Trustees (the Trustees, the Board), the Senate, the Council, Faculty of the College of Commerce and Administration, Dean of the Faculties (but: the faculty); titles like President, Registrar, Professor of Physics, Assistant in Chemistry, Fellow, Scholar; Van Husen Scholarship (but: the scholarship); courses: Political Economy, Autumn Quarter (but: a quarter), First Term (but: two terms; major, minor).

rubrics_metrics.name: 50. Use capitals and small capitals for date/place and salutatory/signature lines in letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Set names of town and state in the date line, salutatory phrase at beginning of letters, and signature/residence at end of letters/articles in capitals and small capitals; format specifics given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: CHICAGO, ILL., January 1, 1911 (set to right, with one em's indention, preferably smaller type). MY DEAR MR. SMITH: (set flush, followed by a colon, same type as body, separate line unless preceded by name/address). CHARLES W. SCOTT (set to the right, with one em's indention, same type as body). HARVARD UNIVERSITY / CAMBRIDGE, MASS. (date formatting guidance and centering notes). See also layout notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: 51. Use 'WHEREAS', 'NOTE', 'SECTION' in resolutions, notes, constitutions/by-laws
rubrics_metrics.description: In resolutions use 'WHEREAS'; in notes (not footnotes) use 'NOTE,' followed by a period and dash; in constitutions/by-laws use 'SECTION' introducing paragraphs followed by a number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: NOTE. — It should be noticed that.... SECTION 1. This association shall be styled.... Usual practice: abbreviate 'SECTION' after first occurrence (e.g., SECTION 1. ...; SEC. 2. ...). See rule 39.

rubrics_metrics.name: 52. Set A.M., P.M., B.C., A.D. in small capitals
rubrics_metrics.description: A.M. and P.M. (ante/post meridiem) and B.C., A.D. should be set in small capitals and without a space between letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 11:30 A.M.; 53 B.C., 1906 A.D.; see also rules 22, 103, 106, 219.

rubrics_metrics.name: 53. Use lower-case initial letter for commonized proper names and derivatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Use small (lower-case) initial for words of common usage originally proper names and their derivatives, and generally all verbs derived from proper names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Utopia (proper), bohemian, philistine, titanic, platonic, quixotic, bonanza, china, morocco, guinea-pig, boycott, roman (type), italicize, anglicize, macadamize. See rule 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: 54. Lower-case for minor subdivisions in literary references
rubrics_metrics.description: Use lower-case for minor subdivisions and their abbreviations in literary references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: chapter, section, page, article, verse, line, note; chap., sec., p., art., vs., l., n. See also rules 37, 90, 237.

rubrics_metrics.name: 55. Lower-case abbreviations for units of measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use lower-case initial abbreviations for units: h.=hour, min.=minute, sec.=second; lb.=pound, oz.=ounce; yd.=yard, ft.=foot; etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: 56. Italic side-heads capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: In italic side-heads, capitalize only the first word and proper names; set other words lower-case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rules 172 and 280 for exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 57. Capitalize first word of a quotation connected to preceding text
rubrics_metrics.description: The first word of a quotation that is immediately connected with what precedes should be capitalized even if in the original it begins a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See illustrations and exception in rules 35 and 131.

rubrics_metrics.name: 58. Italicize words/phrases for emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize words or phrases to which emphasis or importance is desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "This was, however, not the case"; "It is sufficiently plain that the sciences of life, at least, are studies of processes."

rubrics_metrics.name: 59. Italicize foreign words/phrases not incorporated into English
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize words and phrases from foreign languages inserted into English text that are not incorporated into English; also single sentences or brief passages not long enough for reduced type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "the Darwinian Weltanschauung"; "Napoleon's coup d'etat"; "De gustibus non est disputandum". Do not italicize foreign titles preceding names or names of foreign institutions/places whose English equivalent would require roman type (e.g., Pere Lagrange, German Reichstag). Do not italicize foreign words that have become anglicized (e.g., cafe, resume, naive). See list of common foreign terms included.

rubrics_metrics.name: 60. Italicize titles of publications (books, pamphlets, treatises, periodicals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of books (including plays, essays, cycles of poems, single long poems), pamphlets, treatises, tracts, documents, and periodicals should be italicized; newspapers' place-name forms included when integral to name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Spencer, Principles of Sociology; A Midsummer-Night's Dream; Idylls of the King; the Modern Language Review, the Chicago Tribune, the New York Times. Note: Botanical Gazette uses italics in text but roman in footnotes; exceptions for long bibliographical lists, tables (to avoid too many italics). Books of the Bible and titles of ancient manuscripts should be set in roman type; manuscript symbols (Di6, M6, P, J) in roman.

rubrics_metrics.name: 61. Italicize certain Latin/legal abbreviations in references
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize words/phrases and abbreviations used in literary and legal references such as ad loc., circa (ca.), et al., ibid., idem, infra, loc. cit., op. cit., passim, sic, supra, s.v., vide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not italicize cf., e.g., i.e., v. or vs. (versus), viz., etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: 62. Italicize 'See'/'See also' in indices when desirable
rubrics_metrics.description: Use italics (or differentiation) for 'See' and 'See also' in an index or similar compilation when differentiation from context is desirable; also use for 'for' and 'read' in errata lists to separate incorrect and correct readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: See also Sociology; for levee read levee.

rubrics_metrics.name: 63. Italicize names of plaintiff and defendant in legal citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use italics for names of plaintiff and defendant in legal causes and for titles of proceedings containing prefixes like in re, ex parte, In the matter of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Conolly v. Union Sewer Pipe Co.; In re Smith; Ex parte Brown; In the matter of the petition of Henry Robinson for a writ of habeas corpus.

rubrics_metrics.name: 64. Format address lines in speeches/reports/letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Address lines in speeches, reports, etc., and primary address lines in letters should be set flush in a separate line with nouns capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen: Mr. John Smith, 321 Dearborn Street, Chicago, Ill. DEAR SIR: I take pleasure in announcing....

rubrics_metrics.name: 65. Signature titles formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: In signatures, the position or title added after the name: if one word it runs into same line; if more than one but not longer than name center first letter under name and indent one em on right; if longer than name center name over second line and set second line flush. Rules subject to exigencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ARTHUR P. MAGUIRE, Secretary; Yours very truly, CARTER H. HARRISON; Mayor of Chicago / CHARLES M. GAYLEY / Professor of English Language and Literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: 66. Use of a), b), c) etc. for subdivisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a), b), c), etc., to indicate subdivisions (single parenthesis if beginning a paragraph; double parentheses if 'run in'); use a, b, c, etc., affixed to verse/page numbers to denote fractional parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Luke 4:3a.

rubrics_metrics.name: 67. Use letters to designate unknown quantities/lines in technical matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters are used to designate unknown quantities, lines, etc., in algebraic, geometrical, and similar matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ac+bc=c(a+b)^2; the lines ad and AD; the n-th power.

rubrics_metrics.name: 68. Letters in legends or cross-references
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters used in legends or in the text referring to corresponding letters in accompanying illustrations as a rule are set in roman or as specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'At the point A above (see diagram).'

rubrics_metrics.name: 69. References to particular letters
rubrics_metrics.description: References to particular letters are formatted plainly (e.g., the letter «, a small v).

rubrics_metrics.name: 70. s. and d. for shillings and pence following numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 's.' and 'd.' to denote shillings and pence following numerals (see rule 270).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 3s. 6d.

rubrics_metrics.name: 71. Italics for scientific generic and species names when used together (zoological/geological/paleontological)
rubrics_metrics.description: In zoological, geological, and paleontological matter, scientific (Latin) names of genera and species when used together should have the generic name in nominative singular and be italicized; in botanical/geological/paleontological matter names of genera and species together, and genera alone when used alone, italicize; in medical matter generally set in roman avoiding italics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Felis leo, Rosa Carolina, Conodectes favosus, Phyteuma Halleri; single genera: Acer saccharum, Basidiobolus, Alternaria, Erythrosuchus. See rule 46 and notes on astronomical/astrophysical exceptions (a–f).

rubrics_metrics.name: 71a. Astronomical/astrophysical italic exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use italics for Greek, Latin, Arabic names of planets, satellites, constellations, individual stars; catalogue designations; symbols for chemical elements; Fraunhofer spectral capital letters; letters designating spectral types; H with Greek subscripts, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Jupiter, Tethys, Lyra, Antares, λ Orionis; M 13, Bond 619, N.G.C. 6165, 85 Pegasi, Lalande 5761; chemical symbols H, Ca, Ti; spectral letters A–H; spectral types A5, B3, M8; hydrogen lines Ha, Hβ. Initials used as catalogue titles (B.D., N.G.C.) should be italicized.

rubrics_metrics.name: 72. In resolutions use 'Resolved.'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the word 'Resolved.' in resolutions (see rule 39).

rubrics_metrics.name: 73. Use 'Continued' after headlines/titles and 'To be continued' at article ends
rubrics_metrics.description: After headlines or titles use the word 'Continued' as a rule; at the end of articles use 'To be continued.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: THE SCOPE OF SOCIOLOGY— Continued; [To be continued]. See rule 179.

rubrics_metrics.name: 74. Quotation marks for run-in citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Put in quotation marks (roman-quote) and in roman type citations run into the text of a passage from an author in his own words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 85 for block quotation/reduced type rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: 75. Quotation marks for consecutive quotations from different authors/works
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotations from different authors or different works by the same author that follow each other uninterrupted by intervening original matter (or by references other than footnote figures) should be put between quotation marks even if reduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduced quotations exceptions noted in rules 85–87.

rubrics_metrics.name: 76. Quotation marks for word/phrase with definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks (roman) for a word or phrase accompanied by its definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Drop-folio' means a page-number at the foot of the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: 77. Quotation marks for unusual/technical/ironical words or phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for unusual, technical, ironical, or otherwise noteworthy words or phrases in the text, whether or not accompanied by 'so-called' etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Her 'five o' clocks' were famous; She was wearing a gown of 'lobster-colored' silk; He was elected 'master of the rolls'; This so-called 'man of affairs.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 78. Quotation marks for translations
rubrics_metrics.description: In translations, use quotation marks for the English equivalent of a foreign word, phrase, or passage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Weltanschauung, 'world-view' or 'fundamental aspect of life'; Mommsen Romische Geschichte ('History of Rome').

rubrics_metrics.name: 79. Quotation marks to direct attention to particular words
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks to indicate the particular word(s) to which attention is directed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the term 'lynch law'; the phrase 'liberty of conscience'; the concepts 'good' and 'bad'; the name 'Chicago.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 80. Quotation marks for serial titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for serial titles (series titles) and similar compilations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'English Men of Letters' series; 'International Critical Commentary.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 81. Quotation marks for shorter poem titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for titles of shorter poems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Shelley's 'To a Skylark.' See rule 60 for longer poem/book titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: 82. Quotation marks for titles of subdivisions/articles/papers/lectures/sermons/toasts/mottoes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for cited titles of subdivisions of publications and for titles of papers, lectures, sermons, toasts, mottoes, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Beginnings of the Science of Political Economy, Vol. I, 'The British School,' chap. ii, 'John Stuart Mill'; the articles 'Cross,' 'Crucifixion,' and 'Crusade' in Hastings' Dictionary of the Bible; the lecture subject 'Japan — Its Past, Present, and Future'; the toast 'Our German Visitor'; the king's motto is 'For God and My Country.' Note: Botanical Gazette does not use quotation marks for such titles in footnotes. References to Preface/Introduction/Table of Contents/Index etc. of a specific work should be set with capitals without quotation marks: Preface, p. iii; 'The Introduction contains ...' but quoted sentence examples differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: 83. Quotation marks for names of ships
rubrics_metrics.description: Put names of ships in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the U.S. SS. 'Oregon'.

rubrics_metrics.name: 84. Quotation marks for titles of pictures and works of art
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for titles of pictures and works of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Murillo's 'The Holy Family.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 85. Set long prose and poetry extracts in smaller type
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily, set prose extracts that will make five or more lines in smaller type and all poetry citations of two lines or more in smaller type; isolated short prose quotations may be run into text if closely related; short quotations adjacent to longer reduced extracts may be reduced for uniformity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 86 for point-size reductions; see rules 85–87 for exceptions; specific considerations of 'organic relation' and visual uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: 86. Rules for reducing type sizes for citations
rubrics_metrics.description: General point-size reduction guidance: reduce from n-pt and 10-pt to 9-pt; from 9-pt to 8-pt; from 8-pt to 6-pt (see rule 252).

rubrics_metrics.name: 87. Reduced citations should not have quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduced citations (set in smaller type) should not have quotation marks except in cases noted in rule 75; quotation marks generally not used in connection with italics.

rubrics_metrics.name: 88. Quotation marks should include ellipses and 'etc.' when part omitted
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation marks should always include ellipses and the phrase 'etc.' when omission would otherwise be unclear; perfect clearness is the best criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations show cases where 'etc.' is within or outside quotes depending on whether it stands for omitted matter of the quoted passage or for continuation beyond the quote.

rubrics_metrics.name: 89. Repeat opening quotation marks for each paragraph of broken quoted prose
rubrics_metrics.description: If quoted prose broken into paragraphs, repeat the quotation marks at the beginning of each paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: 90. Clear (project) quotation marks for alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Where alignment is desired quotation marks should be 'cleared'—i.e., project beyond the line of alignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example shown with lines: "Keep away from dirtiness — keep away from mess. Don't get into doin' things rather-more-or-less!"

rubrics_metrics.name: 91. Use double quotes for primary quotations and alternate single/double for nested quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Double quotation marks are used for primary quotations; for a quotation within a quotation use single marks; alternate back to double for a third level, single for fourth, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: "The orator then proceeded: 'The dictionary tells us that "the words, 'freedom' and 'liberty,' though often interchanged, are distinct in some of their applications.' '"

rubrics_metrics.name: 92. Spell out religious, civil, military titles of honor and forms of address preceding the name (exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out all religious, civil, and military titles of honor and respect and forms of address preceding the name, except Mr., Messrs., Mrs. (French: M., MM., Mme, Mlle), Dr., Rev., Hon., St.; also abbreviate Esq. following the name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: Do not set Rev., the Hon. except in quotations and correspondence; exceptions listed.

rubrics_metrics.name: 93. Spell out Christian names in ordinary text
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out Christian names (e.g., George, Charles, John) rather than abbreviating (not Geo., Chas., Jno.), except where abbreviated form is used in quoted matter or original signatures; 'von' as part of a person's name is spelled out.

rubrics_metrics.name: 94. Spell out numbers less than three digits in ordinary reading-matter (with exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary reading-matter, spell out all numbers of less than three digits, unless of statistical/technical character or in groups of six or more following each other; treat numbers in connected groups alike; if largest contains three or more digits use figures for all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'There are thirty-eight cities...' 'a fifty-yard dash'; Exceptions: decimals, degrees, dimensions, distances, enumerations, money, percentage, weights generally expressed in figures (10°, 45 miles, 3 cubic feet, 24 pages, $1,000). See rules 95–99 for further detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: 95. Spell out round numbers (approximate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Round numbers (approximate) should be spelled out (unit of 100 under 1,000, unit of 1,000 above), but precise numbers should be in figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The attendance was estimated at five hundred' (but 'at 550'); 'a thesis of about three thousand words' (but 'about 2,700'). For cases like 1,500 spelled out as 'fifteen hundred' rather than 'one thousand five hundred.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 96. Spell out numbers commencing a sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: All numbers, regardless of size, that commence a sentence in ordinary reading-matter should be spelled out; if impracticable, reconstruct the sentence to avoid starting with a numeral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Five hundred and ninety-three men, 417 women, and 126 children...' If impracticable, rewrite as 'The total number ... was 593 men...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: 97. Spell out sums of money in isolated ordinary reading-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Sums of money occurring in isolated cases in ordinary reading-matter should be spelled out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The admission was two dollars.' When several monetary numbers occur together or in statistical contexts use figures: 'Admission: men, $2; women, $1; children, 25 cents.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 98. Time of day expressed in words in ordinary reading-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary reading-matter express time of day in words (at four; at half-past two) unless statistical/enumeration or in connection with A.M./P.M., where use figures (4:15 P.M.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit 'o'clock' in statistical connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: 99. Ages expressed in words
rubrics_metrics.description: Express ages in words: 'eighty years and four months old; children between six and fourteen.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 100. Spell out numbers of centuries, dynasties, sessions, military bodies, political divisions, thoroughfares (unless brevity needed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use spelled-out forms for numbers of centuries, Egyptian dynasties, sessions of Congress, military bodies, political divisions, and similar cases, unless brevity is important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: nineteenth century; Fifth Dynasty; Fifty-fourth Congress, Second Session; Fifteenth Infantry N.G.; Sixth Congressional District; Fifth Avenue. See rules 7, 8, 13 for related guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 101. References to particular decades in words
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to particular decades in words: 'in the nineties.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 102. Names of months spelled out except in statistical or long enumerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out names of months except in statistical matter or in long enumerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'from January 1 to April 15' (omit st, d, th after dates).

rubrics_metrics.name: 103. 'United States' usage guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'United States' in ordinary text except in quotations and certain technical connections (e.g., General Schofield, U.S.A.; U.S. SS. 'Oregon'); in footnotes and similar references use abbreviations like U.S. Geological Survey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rules 22, 52, 106 for related abbreviation guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 104. Use full forms of 'Railroad (-way)', 'Fort', 'Mount', 'Port' in geographical apppellations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Railroad (-way), Fort, Mount, Port as full words in geographical names rather than abbreviations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul Railroad (not R.R. or Ry.); Fort Wayne; Mount Elias; Port Huron.

rubrics_metrics.name: 105. Spell out names of publications in most cases (with flexibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally spell out names of publications in most cases; rule is open to modification based on expediency, context, authoritative usage, and author's preference; if in doubt, spell out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good taste will condone spelling-out offenses more readily than the opposite.

rubrics_metrics.name: 106. Abbreviate names of U.S. states, territories, possessions in lists/bibliographies (no spaces)
rubrics_metrics.description: When following town names in lists, bibliographical matter, etc., abbreviate names of states/territories without spaces between letters (Ala., Ariz., Cal., etc.); not ordinarily abbreviated in running text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rules 22, 52, 103 for cross-references.

rubrics_metrics.name: 107. Abbreviate 'Company' and 'Brothers' and use ampersand in technical/bibliographical references
rubrics_metrics.description: In technical matter (footnotes, bibliographies) use abbreviations for 'Company' and 'Brothers' and the ampersand '&' in names of commercial firms; in ordinary text 'Company' and 'Brothers' may be spelled out; when firm name doesn't consist of proper names spell out 'and'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Macmillan Co., Macmillan & Co., Harper Bros.; Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul Railroad; American Steel and Wire Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: 108. 'Saint' before a name abbreviated to 'St.'; prefer omission for apostles etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'St.' in place of 'Saint' before a name (St. Louis, St. Peter's Church); prefer to omit 'St.' in connection with names of apostles, evangelists, and church fathers (Luke, Paul, Augustine rather than St. Luke, St. Paul).

rubrics_metrics.name: 109. Abbreviations for books of the Bible, Apocrypha, and Bible versions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use prescribed abbreviations for books of the Old and New Testaments, Apocrypha, and commonly referred Bible versions (e.g., Gen., Exod., Matt., Mark; A.V. = Authorized Version; R.V. = Revised Version; A.R.V. = American Standard Revised Version; Vulg. = Vulgate; LXX = Septuagint).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive listing provided for Old Testament, New Testament, Apocrypha, and versions; use the listed abbreviations in citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 110. Abbreviate 'volume', 'number', 'psalm', 'division', 'chapter', 'article', 'section', 'page', 'column', 'verse', 'line', 'note', 'figure' in bibliographical contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: In literary references, footnotes, and bibliographical character, abbreviate words like 'volume' (Vol.), 'number' (No.), 'psalm' (Ps.), 'division' (Div.), 'chapter' (chap.), 'article' (art.), 'section' (sec.), 'page' (p., pp.), 'column' (col.), 'verse' (vs.), 'line' (l.), 'note' (n.), 'Figure' (Fig.), and use constructs like pp. 5–7, pp. 5 f., pp. 5ff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vol. I (Vols.), No. 1 (Nos.), Ps. 20 (Pss.), Div. III, chap. ii (chaps.), art. iii (arts.), sec. 4 (secs.), p. 5 (pp.), col. 6 (cols.), vs. 7 (vss.), l. 8 (ll.), n. 9 (nn.), Fig. 7 (Figs.). Use PP- S~7 (= pages 5 to 7 inclusive), pp. 5 f. (= page 5 and the following page), pp. 5ff. (= page 5 and the following pages).

rubrics_metrics.name: 111. Metric and common measurement abbreviations following a numeral
rubrics_metrics.description: Use metric and common symbols for weights and measures following a numeral: 1 m., 2 dm., 3 cm., 4 mm.; c.m. = cubic meter, c.c., c.mm.; gm. = gram; gr. = grain; h. = hour, min. = minute, sec. = second; lb. = pound, oz. = ounce; yd., ft., in.; A = angstrom units; H.P. = horse-power; C. = centigrade; F. = Fahrenheit; L.C.M. = lowest common multiple; etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 123 for related conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 112. Use office style for modern extracts; preserve originals for Old English or essential renderings
rubrics_metrics.description: In extracts from modern authors whose spelling/punctuation differ slightly from current usage, use office style; in citations from Old English works or where essential to the writer's plan or context, follow the original copy. Titles should always be accurately quoted.

rubrics_metrics.name: 113. Form possessive of proper names ending in -s according to syllable count and pronunciation
rubrics_metrics.description: Form possessive of proper names ending in s or another sibilant: if monosyllabic add apostrophe and s; if more than one syllable add apostrophe alone. For names ending in a silent sibilant, always add apostrophe and s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: King James's Version, Burns's poems, Marx's theories; Moses' law, Jesus' birth, Demosthenes' orations; Charlevoix's discoveries, Des Moines's population.

rubrics_metrics.name: 114. Use 'a' before sounded h, long u (or eu), and words 'one','once'
rubrics_metrics.description: Before sounded h, long u (or eu), and the words 'one,' 'once,' use 'a' as the indefinite article rather than 'an'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a hotel, a harmonic rendition, a historical work, a union, a euphonious word, such a one.

rubrics_metrics.name: 115. Do not use ligatures æ and œ in modern English; retain in Old English and French
rubrics_metrics.description: The ligatures æ and œ are not used currently in Latin/Greek words or adopted English words; write ae, oe, or e alone. Ligatures retained in Old English and French.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: aetas; Oedipus Tyrannus; aesthetic (but oeuvre in French); maneuver; Alfred (English form).

rubrics_metrics.name: 116. Differentiate 'farther' and 'further'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'farther' to mean 'more remote' or 'at a greater distance'; use 'further' to mean 'moreover' or 'in addition'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the farther end; he went still farther; further, he suggested; a further reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: 117. Use 'O' without comma in vocative forms; use 'Oh,' with comma/exclamation for exclamation
rubrics_metrics.description: In forms of address (vocative) use 'O' without a comma following; for exclamation use 'Oh,' followed by comma or exclamation point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'O thou most mighty ruler!' 'Oh, why did not Cerberus drag me back to hell?'. See rule 40.

rubrics_metrics.name: 118. Participles retaining final -e
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain participles retain the final 'e' in the primary word (e.g., agreeing, hieing, singeing; dyeing, hoeing, tingeing; eyeing, shoeing, vieing). Others omit the 'e' before terminal (examples listed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two lists included: participles that retain e and those that omit it; full lists given in examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: 119. Preferred spellings (long list)
rubrics_metrics.description: A comprehensive list of preferred American spellings and single-word forms: many entries provided (e.g., abridgment, accouter, acknowledgment, aluminum, neighbor, color, labor, defense, theater, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note includes instruction: make one word of 'anyone','someone','everyone','today','tomorrow','tonight','cannot'; distinguish 'sometimes' vs 'some time(s)'. Also spelling note: in University of Chicago official publications 'comptroller' spelled as such.

rubrics_metrics.name: 120. Differentiate terminations -ise and -ize
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide lists of verbs/terms that should be spelled with -ise and those with -ize (-yze), specifying which words take which termination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive lists provided. Examples with -ise: advertise, comprise, advise, supervise, etc. Examples with -ize: aggrandize, analyze, authorize, criticize, emphasize, familiarize, organize, realize, etc.; includes many common verbs where -ize is preferred (and exceptions like 'apprise' vs 'apprize' clarified).
